title: Der Königssohn der sich vor nichts fürchtet
titleEn: The King's Son Who Feared Nothing
part: The King's Son Who Feared Nothing
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 121. Text from Wikisource („Der Königssohn der sich vor nichts fürchtet (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 121 follows a king's son who leaves home simply because he is afraid of nothing and wants to see what the world holds. A giant sets him to fetch an apple from the guarded Tree of Life for the giant's bride; he manages it easily, gaining a magic strength-ring and a loyal lion along the way, and the giant's gratitude curdles at once into treachery — he steals the ring by a trick, blinds the prince, and twice tries to lead him to his death over a cliff, foiled each time by the lion, which finally kills the giant outright and helps restore the prince's sight with water from a stream. Healed, the prince and his lion wander on to an enchanted castle, where a beautiful maiden turned black by a curse can only be freed if he survives three midnight visitations of tormenting devils without making a sound; he endures all three, healed each dawn by her water of life as she turns whiter, and on the last morning breaks the spell entirely by swinging his sword three times over the stair, after which the black maiden stands revealed as a rich king's daughter. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as daß, gieng, fieng, ward, Thor and todt.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Königssohn, dem gefiels nicht mehr daheim in seines Vaters Haus,
sentences.l: There was once a king’s-son, to whom it no longer pleased at home in his father’s house,
sentences.i: There was once a king’s son who no longer liked it at home in his father’s house,
sentences.n: gefallen puts the person in the dative — dem gefiels, “to whom it pleased” — so the literal keeps the German shape. gefiels is gefiel es. Königssohn is a glued compound, king + son, which the literal hyphenates to show the joint; seines Vaters Haus is the old genitive standing before its noun.

sentences.t: und weil er vor nichts Furcht hatte, so dachte er „ich will in die weite Welt gehen, da wird mir Zeit und Weile nicht lang, und ich werde wunderliche Dinge genug sehen.“
sentences.l: and because he had fear of nothing, so he thought “I will go into the wide world, there time and while will not grow long for me, and I shall see wondrous things enough.”
sentences.i: and because he was afraid of nothing, he thought, “I will go into the wide world; there the time will not hang heavy on me, and I shall see wonderful things enough.”
sentences.n: vor etwas Furcht haben is “to have fear of a thing,” with vor for what is feared — the tale’s title is built on it. mir wird die Zeit lang is the German for time hanging heavy, again with the person in the dative, and Zeit und Weile doubles the idea. wunderlich is “strange, wondrous,” not the warm modern “wonderful.”

sentences.t: Also nahm er von seinen Eltern Abschied und gieng fort, immer zu, von Morgen bis Abend, und es war ihm einerlei wo hinaus ihn der Weg führte.
sentences.l: So he took leave of his parents and went off, always on, from morning till evening, and it was all one to him where out the way led him.
sentences.i: So he took leave of his parents and went off, ever onward, from morning till evening, and it was all one to him where the way might lead him.
sentences.n: Abschied nehmen is “to take leave.” immer zu is “on and on.” es ist mir einerlei is the set phrase for “it is all one to me,” with the dative once more. wo hinaus, “where out to,” is the old way of asking a direction.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß er vor eines Riesen Haus kam, und weil er müde war, setzte er sich vor die Thüre und ruhte.
sentences.l: It came to pass that he came before a giant’s house, and because he was tired, he set himself before the door and rested.
sentences.i: It came to pass that he came to a giant’s house, and because he was tired he sat down before the door and rested.
sentences.n: sich zutragen, “to come to pass,” is separable and reflexive, and the tales use it constantly. eines Riesen Haus puts the genitive before its noun again. Thüre is the 1857 spelling of Türe, and sich setzen is reflexive where English simply sits down.

sentences.t: Und als er seine Augen so hin und her gehen ließ, sah er auf dem Hof des Riesen Spielwerk liegen:
sentences.l: And when he let his eyes go so to and fro, he saw the giant’s playthings lying in the yard:
sentences.i: And as he let his eyes wander to and fro, he saw the giant’s playthings lying in the yard:
sentences.n: hin und her is “thither and hither,” to and fro. lassen takes a bare infinitive, gehen ließ, “let go,” and so does sehen: sah … liegen, “saw lying.” Spielwerk is an older word for a plaything.

sentences.t: das waren ein paar mächtige Kugeln und Kegel so groß als ein Mensch.
sentences.l: these were a couple of mighty balls and ninepins as big as a man.
sentences.i: these were a couple of mighty balls, and skittles as big as a man.
sentences.n: das waren with a plural verb: das points ahead to what follows. so groß als is the older comparison where the modern language says so groß wie. Kegel are the pins of the bowling game and Kugeln the balls rolled at them.

sentences.t: Über ein Weilchen bekam er Lust, stellte die Kegel auf und schob mit den Kugeln danach, schrie und rief wenn die Kegel fielen, und war guter Dinge.
sentences.l: After a little while he got a desire, set the ninepins up and shoved with the balls after them, shouted and cried when the pins fell, and was of good things.
sentences.i: After a little while the fancy took him: he set the skittles up and bowled the balls at them, shouted and cried out when the pins fell, and was in high spirits.
sentences.n: über ein Weilchen is “after a little while.” schieben is the proper verb for rolling a bowl, and danach, “after them,” closes the clause. guter Dinge sein — “to be of good things” — is the fixed phrase for high spirits, and keeps an old genitive.

sentences.t: Der Riese hörte den Lärm, streckte seinen Kopf zum Fenster heraus und erblickte einen Menschen, der nicht größer war als andere, und doch mit seinen Kegeln spielte.
sentences.l: The giant heard the noise, stretched his head out at the window and caught sight of a person who was not bigger than others, and yet played with his ninepins.
sentences.i: The giant heard the noise, thrust his head out of the window and caught sight of a man who was no bigger than others and yet was playing with his skittles.
sentences.n: zum Fenster heraus doubles the direction — out at the window — as German likes to do. erblicken is a step above sehen: to catch sight of. seinen Kegeln is the giant’s own, and that possessive is the whole grievance.

sentences.t: „Würmchen,“ rief er, „was kegelst du mit meinen Kegeln?
sentences.l: “Little worm,” cried he, “what are you bowling with my ninepins for?
sentences.i: “Little worm,” he cried, “what are you doing bowling with my skittles?
sentences.n: Würmchen is the diminutive of Wurm, said in contempt of something small. kegeln is the verb made straight from the noun, to play at ninepins. was here is the older “why, what for.”

sentences.t: wer hat dir die Stärke dazu gegeben?“
sentences.l: who has given you the strength for it?”
sentences.i: who gave you the strength for that?”
sentences.n: dazu is “to that, for it,” and dir is the dative of the person given to.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn schaute auf, sah den Riesen an und sprach „o du Klotz, du meinst wohl, du hättest allein starke Arme?
sentences.l: The king’s-son looked up, looked at the giant and said “o you block, you think, I suppose, that you alone have strong arms?
sentences.i: The king’s son looked up, looked the giant in the face and said, “oh you lump, you think, do you, that you alone have strong arms?
sentences.n: aufschauen and ansehen are both separable, and both particles fall to the end. Klotz is a block of wood, used of a person as English uses blockhead. wohl in a question is the sceptical “I suppose, do you?”, and hättest is the subjunctive of an opinion quoted back.

sentences.t: ich kann alles, wozu ich Lust habe.“
sentences.l: I can [do] everything to which I have a desire.”
sentences.i: I can do anything I have a mind to.”
sentences.n: können stands alone without a second verb — “I can everything” — so the literal supplies the bracketed [do], which the German does not have. wozu is “to which,” and Lust haben zu is to have a mind for a thing.

sentences.t: Der Riese kam herab, sah dem Kegeln ganz verwundert zu und sprach „Menschenkind, wenn du der Art bist, so geh und hol mir einen Apfel vom Baum des Lebens.“
sentences.l: The giant came down, watched the bowling quite astonished and said “human-child, if you are of that kind, then go and fetch me an apple from the tree of life.”
sentences.i: The giant came down, watched the bowling in astonishment and said, “child of man, if you are of that sort, then go and fetch me an apple from the tree of life.”
sentences.n: zusehen takes the dative of what is watched — sah dem Kegeln … zu — and its particle waits at the end; dem Kegeln is an infinitive used as a noun. Menschenkind, “man-child,” is the giant’s word for a human being and has a Biblical ring. der Art sein is “to be of that kind.”

sentences.t: „Was willst du damit?“ sprach der Königssohn.
sentences.l: “What do you want with it?” said the king’s-son.
sentences.n: wollen is “to want,” not a future, and damit is “with that.”

sentences.t: „Ich will den Apfel nicht für mich,“ antwortete der Riese, „aber ich habe eine Braut, die verlangt danach;
sentences.l: “I do not want the apple for myself,” answered the giant, “but I have a bride, she desires it;
sentences.i: “I do not want the apple for myself,” answered the giant, “but I have a bride, and she longs for it;
sentences.n: die at the head of the second clause is a demonstrative, “she,” not a relative — German carries a sentence on this way. verlangen nach is “to long for,” and danach stands for the apple.

sentences.t: ich bin weit in der Welt umher gegangen und kann den Baum nicht finden.“
sentences.l: I have gone far about in the world and cannot find the tree.”
sentences.i: I have gone far about the world and cannot find the tree.”
sentences.n: umhergehen is separable, and the 1857 text prints the halves apart, umher gegangen. Verbs of motion take sein in the perfect, so it is bin … gegangen.

sentences.t: „Ich will ihn schon finden,“ sagte der Königssohn, „und ich weiß nicht was mich abhalten soll, den Apfel herunter zu holen.“
sentences.l: “I shall find it right enough,” said the king’s-son, “and I do not know what should hold me off from fetching the apple down.”
sentences.i: “I shall find it, never fear,” said the king’s son, “and I do not know what should hinder me from fetching the apple down.”
sentences.n: schon in its reassuring sense again, “right enough.” abhalten is “to hold off, to hinder,” and herunter holen is separable and printed apart. weiß here is the verb wissen, to know.

sentences.t: Der Riese sprach „du meinst wohl das wäre so leicht?
sentences.l: The giant said “you think, I suppose, that would be so easy?
sentences.i: The giant said, “you fancy that would be so easy, do you?
sentences.n: wäre is the subjunctive of a reported opinion — the giant is quoting the prince’s notion back at him — and wohl again marks the sceptical question.

sentences.t: der Garten, worin der Baum steht, ist von einem eisernen Gitter umgeben, und vor dem Gitter liegen wilde Thiere, eins neben dem andern, die halten Wache und lassen keinen Menschen hinein.“
sentences.l: the garden in which the tree stands is surrounded by an iron grating, and before the grating lie wild beasts, one beside the other, they keep watch and let no person in.”
sentences.i: the garden in which the tree stands is surrounded by an iron grating, and before the grating lie wild beasts, one beside the other; they keep watch and let no man in.”
sentences.n: worin is “wherein,” the old relative for in which, and von with the dative names the agent of a passive. die is once more the demonstrative carrying the sentence on, “they,” and hinein closes the clause.

sentences.t: „Mich werden sie schon einlassen,“ sagte der Königssohn.
sentences.l: “Me they will let in right enough,” said the king’s-son.
sentences.i: “They will let me in, never fear,” said the king’s son.
sentences.n: The object leads — Mich — which throws the subject behind the verb; German puts first what matters most, and English can echo it only with the same inversion. einlassen is separable.

sentences.t: „Ja, gelangst du auch in den Garten und siehst den Apfel am Baum hängen, so ist er doch noch nicht dein:
sentences.l: “Yes, even if you get into the garden and see the apple hanging on the tree, it is still not yours yet:
sentences.i: “Yes, and even if you do get into the garden and see the apple hanging on the tree, it is not yours yet:
sentences.n: gelangst du auch … is a concessive with the verb first and no wenn: “even if you do get in.” hängen after siehst is another bare infinitive, and doch is the “still, all the same” that answers the concession.

sentences.t: es hängt ein Ring davor, durch den muß einer die Hand stecken, wenn er den Apfel erreichen und abbrechen will, und das ist noch keinem geglückt.“
sentences.l: there hangs a ring before it, through which one must put the hand, if he wants to reach and break off the apple, and that has succeeded to no one yet.”
sentences.i: a ring hangs before it, and through that ring a man must put his hand if he means to reach the apple and break it off; and that has never yet come off for anyone.”
sentences.n: es hängt ein Ring is the placeholder es with the real subject behind the verb. einer is the indefinite “one, a man.” glücken takes the dative of the person it succeeds for: das ist keinem geglückt.

sentences.t: „Mir solls schon glücken,“ sprach der Königssohn.
sentences.l: “For me it shall succeed right enough,” said the king’s-son.
sentences.i: “It will come off for me, never fear,” said the king’s son.
sentences.n: Mir leads, as Mich did before — the prince answers the giant word for word. solls is soll es, and glücken again takes the dative of the lucky one.

sentences.t: Da nahm er Abschied von dem Riesen, gieng fort über Berg und Thal, durch Felder und Wälder, bis er endlich den Wundergarten fand.
sentences.l: Then he took leave of the giant, went off over hill and dale, through fields and woods, until he at last found the wonder-garden.
sentences.i: Then he took leave of the giant and went off over hill and dale, through fields and woods, until at last he found the wonder-garden.
sentences.n: über Berg und Thal is the fixed travelling formula, “over mountain and valley”; Thal is the 1857 spelling of Tal. Wundergarten is a compound of just its parts, wonder and garden.

sentences.t: Die Thiere lagen rings herum, aber sie hatten die Köpfe gesenkt und schliefen.
sentences.l: The beasts lay round about, but they had their heads lowered and slept.
sentences.i: The beasts lay round about, but their heads were sunk and they slept.
sentences.n: rings herum is “round about, in a ring.” die Köpfe carries no possessive: German leaves the owner understood where English must say “their.” Thiere is the 1857 spelling of Tiere.

sentences.t: Sie erwachten auch nicht, als er heran kam, sondern er trat über sie weg, stieg über das Gitter und kam glücklich in den Garten.
sentences.l: They did not wake either, when he came up, but he stepped away over them, climbed over the grating and came luckily into the garden.
sentences.i: Nor did they wake when he came up: he stepped over them, climbed the grating, and came safely into the garden.
sentences.n: glücklich here is not “happily” but the older “luckily, without mishap” — the same word appears again when he has held out one night. wegtreten über is to step across and away over a thing.

sentences.t: Da stand mitten inne der Baum des Lebens, und die rothen Äpfel leuchteten an den Ästen.
sentences.l: There in the midst stood the tree of life, and the red apples shone on the boughs.
sentences.n: mitten inne is “right in the midst,” inne being the old form that now survives only inside compounds. rothen is the 1857 spelling of roten.

sentences.t: Er kletterte an dem Stamm in die Höhe, und wie er nach einem Apfel reichen wollte, sah er einen Ring davor hängen, aber er steckte seine Hand ohne Mühe hindurch und brach den Apfel.
sentences.l: He climbed up the trunk into the height, and when he wanted to reach for an apple, he saw a ring hanging before it, but he put his hand through without trouble and broke the apple.
sentences.i: He climbed up the trunk, and as he was reaching for an apple he saw a ring hanging before it; but he put his hand through without trouble and broke off the apple.
sentences.n: in die Höhe, “into the height,” is the German for climbing up. nach etwas reichen is to reach for a thing, hindurch closes the clause, and brechen of fruit is simply to pick.

sentences.t: Der Ring schloß sich fest an seinen Arm und er fühlte wie auf einmal eine gewaltige Kraft durch seine Adern drang.
sentences.l: The ring closed itself fast about his arm and he felt how all at once a mighty strength pressed through his veins.
sentences.i: The ring closed tight about his arm, and he felt how all at once a mighty strength went pressing through his veins.
sentences.n: sich schließen an is “to close about.” fühlen wie — “to feel how” — is the German way of feeling a thing happen, where English would rather say “felt a strength press.” dringen is to press or force a way through.

sentences.t: Als er mit dem Apfel von dem Baum wieder herab gestiegen war, wollte er nicht über das Gitter klettern,
sentences.l: When he had climbed down again from the tree with the apple, he did not want to climb over the grating,
sentences.i: When he had climbed down from the tree again with the apple, he would not climb over the grating,
sentences.n: herabsteigen is separable and printed apart in 1857, herab gestiegen; verbs of motion take sein in the perfect. wollte nicht is “would not” — a matter of will, not of ability.

sentences.t: sondern faßte das große Thor und brauchte nur einmal daran zu schütteln, so sprang es mit Krachen auf.
sentences.l: but took hold of the great gate and needed only once to shake at it, and it sprang open with a crash.
sentences.i: but took hold of the great gate, and he needed only to shake it once, and it sprang open with a crash.
sentences.n: nur brauchen zu is “to need only to,” which English keeps almost word for word. an etwas schütteln is to shake at a thing. aufspringen is separable — sprang … auf — and Thor is the 1857 spelling of Tor.

sentences.t: Da gieng er hinaus, und der Löwe, der davor gelegen hatte, war wach geworden und sprang ihm nach, aber nicht in Wuth und Wildheit, sondern er folgte ihm demüthig als seinem Herrn.
sentences.l: Then he went out, and the lion that had lain before it had grown awake and sprang after him, but not in rage and wildness, rather it followed him humbly as its master.
sentences.i: Then he went out, and the lion that had lain before the gate had woken and sprang after him — not in rage and wildness, but following him humbly as its master.
sentences.n: nachspringen is separable and takes the dative, sprang ihm nach; folgen takes the dative too, and als seinem Herrn keeps that same case. wach werden is “to grow awake,” and demüthig is the 1857 spelling of demütig.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn brachte dem Riesen den versprochenen Apfel und sprach „siehst du, ich habe ihn ohne Mühe geholt.“
sentences.l: The king’s-son brought the giant the promised apple and said “you see, I have fetched it without trouble.”
sentences.i: The king’s son brought the giant the promised apple and said, “you see, I have fetched it without any trouble.”
sentences.n: versprochen is a past participle used as an adjective before its noun, a thing German does freely; here it carries the whole bargain. ohne Mühe is “without trouble, without effort.”

sentences.t: Der Riese war froh daß sein Wunsch so bald erfüllt war, eilte zu seiner Braut und gab ihr den Apfel, den sie verlangt hatte.
sentences.l: The giant was glad that his wish was so soon fulfilled, hastened to his bride and gave her the apple that she had desired.
sentences.i: The giant was glad that his wish was so soon fulfilled; he hastened to his bride and gave her the apple she had longed for.
sentences.n: The daß-clause gives the ground of his gladness, and German cannot drop the daß as English drops “that.” war erfüllt uses sein for a state, where English says “had been fulfilled.”

sentences.t: Es war eine schöne und kluge Jungfrau, und da sie den Ring nicht an seinem Arm sah, sprach sie „ich glaube nicht eher daß du den Apfel geholt hast, als bis ich den Ring an deinem Arm erblicke.“
sentences.l: She was a beautiful and clever maiden, and as she did not see the ring on his arm, she said “I do not believe sooner that you have fetched the apple, than until I catch sight of the ring on your arm.”
sentences.i: She was a fair and clever maiden, and since she did not see the ring on his arm, she said, “I shall not believe that you fetched the apple until I see the ring on your arm.”
sentences.n: Es war with a following noun is the German for “she was”; the es is impersonal and points at nothing. nicht eher … als bis is “not sooner … than until,” a doubled turn that English shortens to a plain “until.” da at the head of a clause is “since, as.”

sentences.t: Der Riese sagte „ich brauche nur heim zu gehen und ihn zu holen“ und meinte es wäre ein leichtes dem schwachen Menschen mit Gewalt weg zu nehmen, was er nicht gutwillig geben wollte.
sentences.l: The giant said “I need only go home and fetch it” and thought it would be an easy thing to take from the weak human by force what he would not give willingly.
sentences.i: The giant said, “I need only go home and fetch it,” and thought it an easy thing to take by force from the weak human what he would not give willingly.
sentences.n: ein leichtes is an adjective used as a noun, “an easy [thing].” wegnehmen is separable and takes the dative of the person robbed, dem schwachen Menschen; the 1857 text prints weg zu nehmen in three pieces. wäre is the subjunctive of what he supposed.

sentences.t: Er forderte also den Ring von ihm, aber der Königssohn weigerte sich.
sentences.l: So he demanded the ring from him, but the king’s-son refused.
sentences.n: fordern von is “to demand of.” sich weigern is reflexive in German where English simply refuses.

sentences.t: „Wo der Apfel ist muß auch der Ring sein,“ sprach der Riese, „gibst du ihn nicht gutwillig, so mußt du mit mir darum kämpfen.“
sentences.l: “Where the apple is the ring must be too,” said the giant, “if you do not give it willingly, then you must fight with me for it.”
sentences.i: “Where the apple is, the ring must be too,” said the giant; “if you do not give it up willingly, then you must fight me for it.”
sentences.n: gibst du ihn nicht … is again a conditional with the verb first and no wenn. darum is “for it, about it,” naming the thing fought over, and gutwillig is “of good will, willingly.”

sentences.t: Sie rangen lange Zeit mit einander, aber der Riese konnte dem Königssohn, den die Zauberkraft des Ringes stärkte, nichts anhaben.
sentences.l: They wrestled a long time with one another, but the giant could do nothing to the king’s-son, whom the magic power of the ring strengthened.
sentences.i: They wrestled a long while together, but the giant could do nothing against the king’s son, whom the magic power of the ring made strong.
sentences.n: ringen is “to wrestle,” its past rangen. jemandem nichts anhaben können is the set phrase for being unable to harm someone, and anhaben is separable, its an waiting to the end. The relative clause is pushed inside the main one, which German can hold open in a way English cannot.

sentences.t: Da sann der Riese auf eine List und sprach „mir ist warm geworden bei dem Kampf, und dir auch, wir wollen im Flusse baden und uns abkühlen, eh wir wieder anfangen.“
sentences.l: Then the giant thought upon a trick and said “it has grown warm to me in the fight, and to you too, we will bathe in the river and cool ourselves, before we begin again.”
sentences.i: Then the giant hit on a trick and said, “I have grown warm with the fighting, and you too; let us bathe in the river and cool off before we begin again.”
sentences.n: auf etwas sinnen is “to think upon, to plot” a thing, its past sann. mir ist warm geworden is impersonal, with the person in the dative — “it has grown warm to me” — which the literal keeps. Flusse holds the old dative -e, and eh is the short form of ehe, “before.”

sentences.t: Der Königssohn, der von Falschheit nichts wußte, gieng mit ihm zu dem Wasser, streifte mit seinen Kleidern auch den Ring vom Arm und sprang in den Fluß.
sentences.l: The king’s-son, who knew nothing of falseness, went with him to the water, stripped off with his clothes the ring too from his arm and sprang into the river.
sentences.i: The king’s son, who knew nothing of treachery, went with him to the water, and with his clothes he stripped the ring from his arm as well, and sprang into the river.
sentences.n: von etwas wissen is “to know of a thing.” streifen is to strip a thing off with a sliding motion, and the little auch is what matters: the ring comes away with the clothes, and the tale lets the disaster pass in half a line.

sentences.t: Alsbald griff der Riese nach dem Ring und lief damit fort,
sentences.l: At once the giant reached for the ring and ran off with it,
sentences.n: alsbald is the old “straightway.” nach etwas greifen is to grasp at a thing, and fortlaufen is separable, its fort at the end.

sentences.t: aber der Löwe, der den Diebstahl bemerkt hatte, setzte dem Riesen nach, riß den Ring ihm aus der Hand und brachte ihn seinem Herrn zurück.
sentences.l: but the lion, which had noticed the theft, set after the giant, tore the ring out of his hand and brought it back to his master.
sentences.i: but the lion, which had marked the theft, set after the giant, tore the ring out of his hand, and brought it back to its master.
sentences.n: nachsetzen takes the dative: setzte dem Riesen nach. ihm aus der Hand is the dative of the person concerned again, where English says “out of his hand.” zurückbringen is separable.

sentences.t: Da stellte sich der Riese hinter einen Eichbaum, und als der Königssohn beschäftigt war seine Kleider wieder anzuziehen, überfiel er ihn und stach ihm beide Augen aus.
sentences.l: Then the giant placed himself behind an oak tree, and when the king’s-son was busy putting his clothes on again, he fell upon him and stabbed both his eyes out.
sentences.i: Then the giant placed himself behind an oak, and when the king’s son was busy putting his clothes on again, he fell upon him and struck out both his eyes.
sentences.n: sich stellen is “to place oneself.” überfallen is inseparable and means to fall upon, to attack unawares. ausstechen is separable, “to put out” an eye, and takes the dative of the person: stach ihm … aus. The tale reports the blinding as flatly as the dressing, and it should not be softened.

sentences.t: Nun stand da der arme Königssohn, war blind und wußte sich nicht zu helfen.
sentences.l: Now there stood the poor king’s-son, was blind and did not know how to help himself.
sentences.i: Now there stood the poor king’s son, blind and not knowing how to help himself.
sentences.n: sich zu helfen wissen is “to know how to help oneself,” the German for knowing what to do. The subject is not repeated before war — one subject can carry two verbs.

sentences.t: Da kam der Riese wieder herbei, faßte ihn bei der Hand, wie jemand der ihn leiten wollte, und führte ihn auf die Spitze eines hohen Felsens.
sentences.l: Then the giant came up again, took him by the hand, like someone who wanted to lead him, and led him onto the top of a high rock.
sentences.i: Then the giant came up again, took him by the hand like one who meant to guide him, and led him to the top of a high rock.
sentences.n: bei der Hand fassen is “to take by the hand,” with bei where English says “by.” Felsens is the genitive of Fels, a rock or crag.

sentences.t: Dann ließ er ihn stehen, und dachte „noch ein paar Schritte weiter, so stürzt er sich todt, und ich kann ihm den Ring abziehen.“
sentences.l: Then he let him stand, and thought “a couple of steps further, and he plunges himself dead, and I can draw the ring off him.”
sentences.i: Then he left him standing there and thought, “a couple of steps further, and he will fall to his death, and I can draw the ring off him.”
sentences.n: stehen lassen is “to leave standing.” sich todt stürzen — “to plunge oneself dead” — is the German for falling to one’s death, and todt is the 1857 spelling of tot. abziehen is separable and takes the dative, ihm … abziehen.

sentences.t: Aber der treue Löwe hatte seinen Herrn nicht verlassen, hielt ihn am Kleide fest und zog ihn allmälig wieder zurück.
sentences.l: But the faithful lion had not forsaken its master, held him fast by the garment and drew him gradually back again.
sentences.i: But the faithful lion had not forsaken its master; it held him fast by his coat and drew him gradually back again.
sentences.n: festhalten and zurückziehen are both separable. am Kleide keeps the old dative -e, and allmälig is the 1857 spelling of allmählich.

sentences.t: Als der Riese kam und den Todten berauben wollte, sah er daß seine List vergeblich gewesen war.
sentences.l: When the giant came and wanted to rob the dead man, he saw that his trick had been in vain.
sentences.i: When the giant came and meant to rob the dead man, he saw that his trick had been in vain.
sentences.n: den Todten is an adjective used as a noun, “the dead one” — the giant is taking for granted what has not happened. berauben takes the accusative of the person robbed.

sentences.t: „Ist denn ein so schwaches Menschenkind nicht zu verderben!“ sprach er zornig zu sich selbst, faßte den Königssohn und führte ihn auf einem andern Weg nochmals zu dem Abgrund:
sentences.l: “Is such a weak human-child then not to be destroyed!” he said angrily to himself, took hold of the king’s-son and led him by another way once more to the abyss:
sentences.i: “Is a human child so weak as this not to be destroyed, then!” he said angrily to himself, took hold of the king’s son and led him by another way once more to the abyss:
sentences.n: nicht zu verderben sein is the sein + zu turn, “not to be destroyed,” where English needs a passive. denn in a question is the impatient “then, after all.” The 1857 text sets an exclamation mark where we might put a question mark: the older punctuation follows the tone rather than the grammar.

sentences.t: aber der Löwe, der die böse Absicht merkte, half seinem Herrn auch hier aus der Gefahr.
sentences.l: but the lion, which marked the evil intention, helped its master out of the danger here too.
sentences.i: but the lion, which marked the evil intent, helped its master out of danger here as well.
sentences.n: helfen takes the dative: half seinem Herrn. merken is “to notice, to mark,” and the lion does the noticing the blind man cannot.

sentences.t: Als sie nahe zum Rand gekommen waren, ließ der Riese die Hand des Blinden fahren und wollte ihn allein zurücklassen,
sentences.l: When they had come near to the edge, the giant let the blind man’s hand go and wanted to leave him alone,
sentences.i: When they had come near the edge, the giant let go the blind man’s hand and meant to leave him there alone,
sentences.n: fahren lassen is the set phrase for letting go of what one is holding; the fahren has nothing to do with travelling. des Blinden is another adjective used as a noun, “of the blind one,” and zurücklassen is separable.

sentences.t: aber der Löwe stieß den Riesen, daß er hinab stürzte und zerschmettert auf den Boden fiel.
sentences.l: but the lion thrust the giant, so that he plunged down and fell shattered on the ground.
sentences.i: but the lion thrust the giant so that he plunged down and fell shattered on the ground.
sentences.n: The daß-clause gives the consequence, “so that.” hinab stürzen is printed apart in 1857, and zerschmettert, the past participle of zerschmettern, describes how he lands rather than what is done to him.

sentences.t: Das treue Thier zog seinen Herrn wieder von dem Abgrund zurück und leitete ihn zu einem Baum, an dem ein klarer Bach floß.
sentences.l: The faithful beast drew its master back again from the abyss and led him to a tree, by which a clear brook flowed.
sentences.i: The faithful beast drew its master back from the abyss again and led him to a tree by which a clear brook flowed.
sentences.n: zurückziehen is separable once more. an dem is “by which,” with an for a thing running alongside, and Thier is the 1857 spelling of Tier.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn setzte sich da nieder, der Löwe aber legte sich und spritzte mit seiner Tatze ihm das Wasser ins Antlitz.
sentences.l: The king’s-son set himself down there, but the lion laid itself down and splashed the water with its paw into his countenance.
sentences.i: The king’s son sat down there, and the lion lay down and splashed the water into his face with its paw.
sentences.n: sich niedersetzen and sich legen are both reflexive where English simply sits or lies down. ihm is the dative of the person concerned, and Antlitz is the elevated word for the face, which the tale keeps for this moment.

sentences.t: Kaum hatten ein paar Tröpfchen die Augenhöhlen benetzt, so konnte er wieder etwas sehen und bemerkte ein Vöglein, das flog ganz nah vorbei, stieß sich aber an einen Baumstamm:
sentences.l: Hardly had a couple of little drops wetted the eye-sockets, and he could see something again and noticed a little bird, it flew quite close past, but struck itself against a tree trunk:
sentences.i: Hardly had a few little drops wetted his eye-sockets before he could see something again, and he noticed a little bird: it flew close by, but struck itself against a tree trunk:
sentences.n: Kaum … so … is the old “hardly had … when,” with the verb first after kaum. Tröpfchen and Vöglein are diminutives of Tropfen and Vogel. das begins a new clause as a demonstrative, “it,” not a relative, and sich stoßen an is to knock oneself against a thing.

sentences.t: hierauf ließ es sich in das Wasser herab und badete sich darin, dann flog es auf, strich ohne anzustoßen zwischen den Bäumen hin, als hätte es sein Gesicht wieder bekommen.
sentences.l: thereupon it let itself down into the water and bathed itself in it, then it flew up, swept along between the trees without striking, as if it had got its sight back again.
sentences.i: thereupon it let itself down into the water and bathed in it, then flew up and swept along between the trees without striking anything, as though it had got its sight back.
sentences.n: sich herablassen is “to let oneself down.” hinstreichen is separable, and streichen of a bird is to sweep or skim along — not the streichen of spreading. Gesicht here is not the face but the older sense, eyesight: sein Gesicht wieder bekommen, “to get one’s sight back.” The bird tells the prince what to do without a word.

sentences.t: Da erkannte der Königssohn den Wink Gottes, neigte sich herab zu dem Wasser und wusch und badete sich darin das Gesicht.
sentences.l: Then the king’s-son recognised the beckoning of God, bent himself down to the water and washed and bathed his face in it.
sentences.i: Then the king’s son knew it for a sign from God, bent down to the water, and washed and bathed his face in it.
sentences.n: Wink is a nod or a beckoning — a sign given rather than a word spoken. sich neigen is reflexive, “to bend oneself.” sich das Gesicht waschen puts the reflexive in the dative and the face in the accusative, which is how German says washing one’s own face; and here Gesicht is the face again, not the sight of the line before.

sentences.t: Und als er sich aufrichtete, hatte er seine Augen wieder so hell und rein, wie sie nie gewesen waren.
sentences.l: And when he raised himself up, he had his eyes again so bright and clear as they had never been.
sentences.i: And when he raised himself up, his eyes were again as bright and clear as they had never been before.
sentences.n: sich aufrichten is “to set oneself upright.” The comparison outdoes itself — so hell und rein, wie sie nie gewesen waren, brighter than they had ever been.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn dankte Gott für die große Gnade und zog mit seinem Löwen weiter in der Welt herum.
sentences.l: The king’s-son thanked God for the great mercy and journeyed on about the world with his lion.
sentences.i: The king’s son thanked God for the great mercy, and journeyed on about the world with his lion.
sentences.n: danken takes the dative of the person thanked. Gnade is grace or mercy shown from above. herumziehen is separable, and weiter … herum spreads the wandering across the whole clause.

sentences.t: Nun trug es sich zu daß er vor ein Schloß kam, welches verwünscht war.
sentences.l: Now it came to pass that he came before a castle which was under a curse.
sentences.i: Now it came to pass that he came to a castle which was under a spell.
sentences.n: sich zutragen again, “to come to pass.” welches is the older relative pronoun where the modern language says das. verwünscht is “cursed, enchanted” — built on wünschen, to wish, a wish turned the wrong way.

sentences.t: In dem Thor stand eine Jungfrau von schöner Gestalt und feinem Antlitz, aber sie war ganz schwarz.
sentences.l: In the gate stood a maiden of fair form and fine countenance, but she was quite black.
sentences.i: In the gateway stood a maiden of fair form and fine countenance, but she was quite black.
sentences.n: von schöner Gestalt is the German way of describing a person by a quality, “of fair form.” The blackness is the mark of the enchantment, and the tale will measure her release by how far the whiteness has spread — her feet first, then to the fingertips, then all of her.

sentences.t: Sie redete ihn an und sprach „ach, könntest du mich erlösen aus dem bösen Zauber, der über mich geworfen ist.“
sentences.l: She spoke to him and said “ah, if you could release me from the evil spell that is thrown over me.”
sentences.i: She addressed him and said, “ah, if only you could release me from the evil spell that is cast over me.”
sentences.n: anreden is separable, “to address.” könntest du … is a wish with the verb first and no wenn, “if only you could.” einen Zauber über jemanden werfen is to cast a spell over someone, and the German keeps the throwing.

sentences.t: „Was soll ich thun?“ sprach der Königssohn.
sentences.l: “What am I to do?” said the king’s-son.
sentences.n: soll is “am I to,” asking what is expected of him, not what he ought morally to do. thun is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: Die Jungfrau antwortete „drei Nächte mußt du in dem großen Saal des verwünschten Schlosses zubringen, aber es darf keine Furcht in dein Herz kommen.
sentences.l: The maiden answered “three nights you must pass in the great hall of the enchanted castle, but no fear may come into your heart.
sentences.i: The maiden answered, “three nights you must pass in the great hall of the enchanted castle, but no fear may come into your heart.
sentences.n: The time expression leads — drei Nächte — which puts the verb second and the subject after it. zubringen of time is “to pass, to spend.” dürfen is not ability but permission: no fear is allowed in.

sentences.t: Wenn sie dich auf das ärgste quälen und du hältst es aus ohne einen Laut von dir zu geben, so bin ich erlöst;
sentences.l: If they torment you in the worst way and you hold it out without giving a sound from you, then I am released;
sentences.i: If they torment you in the worst way and you hold out without giving a sound, then I am released;
sentences.n: auf das ärgste is a superlative used adverbially, “in the worst manner.” The second half slips out of the subordinate order into the main one — und du hältst es aus — which spoken German does easily. aushalten is separable, and einen Laut von sich geben is “to give a sound from oneself.”

sentences.t: das Leben dürfen sie dir nicht nehmen.“
sentences.l: your life they may not take from you.”
sentences.i: your life they are not allowed to take.”
sentences.n: The object leads again — das Leben — with the subject after the verb. dir is the dative of the person deprived, where English says “your life,” and dürfen is once more permission, not ability.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Königssohn „ich fürchte mich nicht, ich wills mit Gottes Hülfe versuchen.“
sentences.l: Then the king’s-son said “I do not fear, I will try it with God’s help.”
sentences.i: Then the king’s son said, “I am not afraid; I will try it with God’s help.”
sentences.n: sich fürchten is reflexive, “to fear oneself,” and it is the verb of the tale’s title — der sich vor nichts fürchtet. wills is will es, and Hülfe is the 1857 spelling of Hilfe.

sentences.t: Also gieng er fröhlich in das Schloß, und als es dunkel ward, setzte er sich in den großen Saal und wartete.
sentences.l: So he went cheerfully into the castle, and when it grew dark, he set himself in the great hall and waited.
sentences.i: So he went cheerfully into the castle, and when it grew dark he sat down in the great hall and waited.
sentences.n: es ward dunkel is impersonal, “it grew dark,” with ward the old past of werden. sich setzen in takes the accusative because he moves into the place.

sentences.t: Es war aber still bis Mitternacht, da fieng plötzlich ein großer Lärm an, und aus allen Ecken und Winkeln kamen kleine Teufel herbei.
sentences.l: But it was still until midnight, then suddenly a great noise began, and out of all corners and nooks little devils came up.
sentences.i: But it was still until midnight; then suddenly a great noise began, and out of every corner and cranny little devils came up.
sentences.n: anfangen is separable — fieng … an — and fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing. Ecken und Winkeln is a paired phrase, corners and nooks, and herbeikommen is separable too, its herbei closing the clause.

sentences.t: Sie thaten als ob sie ihn nicht sähen, setzten sich mitten in die Stube, machten ein Feuer an und fiengen an zu spielen.
sentences.l: They did as if they did not see him, set themselves in the middle of the room, made a fire and began to play.
sentences.i: They behaved as though they did not see him, sat down in the middle of the room, lit a fire and began to play.
sentences.n: thun als ob is “to act as if,” and sähen is the subjunctive that goes with it. anmachen is “to light” a fire; both anmachen and anfangen leave their an at the end. thaten is the 1857 spelling of taten.

sentences.t: Wenn einer verlor, sprach er „es ist nicht richtig, es ist einer da, der nicht zu uns gehört, der ist Schuld, daß ich verliere.“
sentences.l: Whenever one lost, he said “it is not right, there is one here who does not belong to us, he is to blame that I lose.”
sentences.i: Whenever one of them lost, he said, “this is not right; there is one here who does not belong to us, and he is to blame that I lose.”
sentences.n: wenn here is “whenever,” the repeated occasion. es ist einer da is the placeholder es with the real subject behind it, and Schuld sein is “to be to blame.”

sentences.t: „Wart ich komme, du hinter dem Ofen,“ sagte ein anderer.
sentences.l: “Wait, I am coming, you behind the stove,” said another.
sentences.n: wart is the imperative of warten with its -e dropped. du hinter dem Ofen is an address, “you there behind the stove” — the corner behind the tiled stove is the warmest and best hidden place in an old room.

sentences.t: Das Schreien ward immer größer, so daß es niemand ohne Schrecken hätte anhören können.
sentences.l: The screaming grew ever greater, so that nobody could have listened to it without terror.
sentences.i: The screaming grew louder and louder, so that no one could have listened to it without terror.
sentences.n: das Schreien is an infinitive used as a noun. immer with a comparative is “ever, more and more.” hätte … anhören können is the past subjunctive of possibility, with both infinitives at the end in the German order.

sentences.t: Der Königssohn blieb ganz ruhig sitzen und hatte keine Furcht:
sentences.l: The king’s-son remained sitting quite quietly and had no fear:
sentences.n: sitzen bleiben is “to remain sitting,” with a bare infinitive after bleiben.

sentences.t: doch endlich sprangen die Teufel von der Erde auf und fielen über ihn her, und es waren so viele, daß er sich ihrer nicht erwehren konnte.
sentences.l: but at last the devils sprang up from the ground and fell upon him, and there were so many that he could not defend himself of them.
sentences.i: but at last the devils sprang up from the ground and fell upon him, and there were so many of them that he could not fend them off.
sentences.n: aufspringen and herfallen über are both separable, their auf and her falling to the end. sich erwehren takes the genitive — sich ihrer erwehren, “to defend oneself of them” — an old case-use that has nearly gone from the language.

sentences.t: Sie zerrten ihn auf dem Boden herum, zwickten, stachen, schlugen und quälten ihn, aber er gab keinen Laut von sich.
sentences.l: They dragged him about on the ground, pinched, stabbed, beat and tormented him, but he gave no sound from himself.
sentences.i: They dragged him about on the ground, pinched, stabbed, beat and tormented him, but he gave no sound.
sentences.n: herumzerren is separable, herum closing the clause. Four bare verbs stand in a row with a single object at the end: the German keeps the beating short and lets the list do the work.

sentences.t: Gegen Morgen verschwanden sie, und er war so abgemattet, daß er kaum seine Glieder regen konnte:
sentences.l: Toward morning they vanished, and he was so worn out that he could hardly stir his limbs:
sentences.i: Towards morning they vanished, and he was so worn out that he could scarcely stir his limbs:
sentences.n: gegen with a time is “toward.” abgemattet is the past participle of abmatten, to wear out. regen is “to stir,” and survives now mostly in sich regen.

sentences.t: als aber der Tag anbrach, da trat die schwarze Jungfrau zu ihm herein.
sentences.l: but when the day broke, the black maiden stepped in to him.
sentences.n: anbrechen, “to break” of day, is separable. hereintreten zu is “to step in to” a person, with herein at the end.

sentences.t: Sie trug in ihrer Hand eine kleine Flasche, worin Wasser des Lebens war, damit wusch sie ihn, und alsbald fühlte er wie alle Schmerzen verschwanden und frische Kraft in seine Adern drang.
sentences.l: She carried in her hand a little flask in which was water of life, with that she washed him, and at once he felt how all pains vanished and fresh strength pressed into his veins.
sentences.i: She carried in her hand a little flask in which was the water of life; with it she washed him, and at once he felt how all his pains vanished and fresh strength went pressing into his veins.
sentences.n: worin is the old “wherein” and damit is “with that.” Wasser des Lebens stands without an article, as a name for the thing. fühlen wie again for feeling something happen.

sentences.t: Sie sprach „eine Nacht hast du glücklich ausgehalten, aber noch zwei stehen dir bevor.“
sentences.l: She said “one night you have held out luckily, but two still stand before you.”
sentences.i: She said, “one night you have come through, but two still lie before you.”
sentences.n: The object leads — eine Nacht — with the verb second. glücklich is again “luckily, safely,” not “happily.” bevorstehen is separable and takes the dative: stehen dir bevor, “are still before you.”

sentences.t: Da gieng sie wieder weg, und im Weggehen bemerkte er daß ihre Füße weiß geworden waren.
sentences.l: Then she went away again, and in the going-away he noticed that her feet had grown white.
sentences.i: Then she went away again, and as she went he noticed that her feet had grown white.
sentences.n: weggehen is separable, and im Weggehen is that same verb turned into a noun, “in the going away.” weiß here is the colour, and the measure of the enchantment: her feet first.

sentences.t: In der folgenden Nacht kamen die Teufel und fiengen ihr Spiel aufs neue an:
sentences.l: On the following night the devils came and began their game anew:
sentences.n: aufs neue is “anew, afresh.” anfangen is separable again — fiengen … an — with the object standing in between.

sentences.t: sie fielen über den Königssohn her und schlugen ihn viel härter als in der vorigen Nacht, daß sein Leib voll Wunden war.
sentences.l: they fell upon the king’s-son and beat him much harder than in the previous night, so that his body was full of wounds.
sentences.i: they fell upon the king’s son and beat him far harder than the night before, so that his body was full of wounds.
sentences.n: herfallen über once more. daß here stands for so daß, “so that,” with the so left out — the consequence follows bare.

sentences.t: Doch da er alles still ertrug, mußten sie von ihm lassen, und als die Morgenröthe anbrach, erschien die Jungfrau und heilte ihn mit dem Lebenswasser.
sentences.l: But since he bore everything silently, they had to leave off from him, and when the dawn-red broke, the maiden appeared and healed him with the life-water.
sentences.i: But since he bore it all in silence, they had to let him be; and when the red of dawn broke, the maiden appeared and healed him with the water of life.
sentences.n: da at the head of a clause is “since, because.” von jemandem lassen is “to leave off from someone.” Morgenröthe is the red of the morning sky (Röthe is the 1857 spelling of Röte), and Lebenswasser is the same water of life glued into one word.

sentences.t: Und als sie weggieng, sah er mit Freuden daß sie schon weiß geworden war bis zu den Fingerspitzen.
sentences.l: And when she went away, he saw with joy that she had already grown white up to the fingertips.
sentences.i: And when she went away, he saw with joy that she had already grown white as far as her fingertips.
sentences.n: mit Freuden keeps the old plural, “with joys.” bis zu den Fingerspitzen measures how far the release has reached: the second night has whitened all but the last of her.

sentences.t: Nun hatte er nur noch eine Nacht auszuhalten, aber die war die schlimmste.
sentences.l: Now he had only one night more to hold out, but that one was the worst.
sentences.n: haben … zu with an infinitive is “to have something to do.” auszuhalten puts the zu inside the separable verb, aus-zu-halten, and die is the demonstrative, “that one.”

sentences.t: Der Teufelsspuk kam wieder:
sentences.l: The devils’ haunting came again:
sentences.i: The devilish haunting came again:
sentences.n: Spuk is a haunting, a ghostly din; Teufelsspuk glues it to the devils. The colon carries the sentence straight on into their shouting.

sentences.t: „bist du noch da?“ schrien sie, „du sollst gepeinigt werden daß dir der Athem stehen bleibt.“
sentences.l: “are you still there?” they screamed, “you shall be tormented so that the breath stops for you.”
sentences.i: “are you still there?” they screamed; “you shall be tormented till your breath stops.”
sentences.n: gepeinigt werden is the passive of peinigen, to torment, a word built on Pein, pain. daß again stands for so daß. dir der Athem is the dative of the person concerned where English uses a possessive, and Athem is the 1857 spelling of Atem.

sentences.t: Sie stachen und schlugen ihn, warfen ihn hin und her und zogen ihn an Armen und Beinen, als wollten sie ihn zerreißen:
sentences.l: They stabbed and beat him, threw him to and fro and pulled him by arms and legs, as if they wanted to tear him apart:
sentences.i: They stabbed and beat him, threw him this way and that, and pulled him by the arms and legs as though they meant to tear him in pieces:
sentences.n: hin und her again, “to and fro.” als wollten sie is a comparison with the verb first and no wenn, “as if they wanted to.” an Armen und Beinen goes without an article, which makes the phrase blunt.

sentences.t: aber er duldete alles und gab keinen Laut von sich.
sentences.l: but he suffered everything and gave no sound from himself.
sentences.i: but he bore it all and gave no sound.
sentences.n: dulden is “to suffer, to endure” without resisting, and it is the whole condition laid on him: silence under whatever comes.

sentences.t: Endlich verschwanden die Teufel, aber er lag da ohnmächtig und regte sich nicht:
sentences.l: At last the devils vanished, but he lay there in a swoon and did not stir himself:
sentences.i: At last the devils vanished, but he lay there in a swoon and did not stir:
sentences.n: ohnmächtig is “powerless, fainting,” from ohne Macht. sich regen is “to stir oneself,” reflexive where English is not.

sentences.t: er konnte auch nicht die Augen aufheben, um die Jungfrau zu sehen, die herein kam und ihn mit dem Wasser des Lebens benetzte und begoß.
sentences.l: he could not lift his eyes either, to see the maiden who came in and wetted him and poured over him with the water of life.
sentences.i: nor could he lift his eyes to see the maiden, who came in and wetted him and poured the water of life over him.
sentences.n: aufheben is “to lift up,” and um … zu is the purpose clause, “in order to.” benetzen is to moisten and begießen to pour over; the two together say she did it thoroughly.

sentences.t: Aber auf einmal war er von allen Schmerzen befreit und fühlte sich frisch und gesund, als wäre er aus einem Schlaf erwacht,
sentences.l: But all at once he was freed from all pains and felt himself fresh and sound, as if he had awakened out of a sleep,
sentences.i: But all at once he was freed from all his pains and felt fresh and sound, as though he had awakened out of a sleep,
sentences.n: auf einmal is “all at once.” sich fühlen is reflexive where English simply feels, and als wäre er … is once more the comparison with the verb first.

sentences.t: und wie er die Augen aufschlug, so sah er die Jungfrau neben sich stehen, die war schneeweiß und schön, wie der helle Tag.
sentences.l: and when he struck his eyes open, he saw the maiden standing beside him, she was snow-white and fair, like the bright day.
sentences.i: and when he opened his eyes, he saw the maiden standing beside him: she was snow-white and fair as the bright day.
sentences.n: die Augen aufschlagen — “to strike the eyes open” — is the German for opening them, and the literal keeps the blow in it. die is the demonstrative again, “she.” The enchantment is counted out to the end: black at the gate, white to the fingertips, and now snow-white all over.

sentences.t: „Steh auf,“ sprach sie, „und schwing dein Schwert dreimal über die Treppe, so ist alles erlöst.“
sentences.l: “Stand up,” she said, “and swing your sword three times over the stair, and everything is released.”
sentences.i: “Get up,” she said, “and swing your sword three times over the stair, and all is released.”
sentences.n: aufstehen is separable, steh … auf, and schwing is the imperative of schwingen. so ist alles erlöst states the consequence as a fact: the deed and its effect in one breath.

sentences.t: Und als er das gethan hatte, da war das ganze Schloß vom Zauber befreit, und die Jungfrau war eine reiche Königstochter.
sentences.l: And when he had done that, the whole castle was freed from the spell, and the maiden was a rich king’s-daughter.
sentences.i: And when he had done that, the whole castle was freed from the spell, and the maiden was a rich king’s daughter.
sentences.n: gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan. war … befreit uses sein for the resulting state. Königstochter is the same glued compound as Königssohn, standing at the other end of the tale.

sentences.t: Die Diener kamen und sagten im großen Saale wäre die Tafel schon zubereitet und die Speisen aufgetragen.
sentences.l: The servants came and said in the great hall the table was already prepared and the dishes served up.
sentences.i: The servants came and said that in the great hall the table was already laid and the dishes served.
sentences.n: wäre is the subjunctive of reported speech, and German needs no daß to introduce it — the mood alone shows that this is what they said. Saale keeps the old dative -e, and auftragen is “to carry up, to serve” a meal.

sentences.t: Da setzten sie sich nieder, aßen und tranken zusammen, und Abends ward in großen Freuden die Hochzeit gefeiert.
sentences.l: Then they set themselves down, ate and drank together, and in the evening the wedding was celebrated in great joys.
sentences.i: Then they sat down, ate and drank together, and in the evening the wedding was celebrated with great rejoicing.
sentences.n: Abends is a genitive of time, “of an evening.” in großen Freuden keeps the old plural of Freude, and ward is the old past of werden making the passive. The tale ends, as so many do, at the table and the wedding.

glossary.blinden: der Blinde — the blind man (adjective used as a noun, gen. sg.: die Hand des Blinden)
glossary.eins: eins — one (neuter; eins neben dem andern: one beside the other)
glossary.fest: fest — firm, tight (adj./adv.; festhalten: to hold fast; fest glauben: to believe firmly)
glossary.gesicht: das Gesicht — face; also, in the older sense, sight, eyesight (sein Gesicht wieder bekommen: to get one’s sight back)
glossary.laut: der Laut — a sound (noun; einen Laut von sich geben: to utter a sound — beside the adjective laut, “loud”)
glossary.reichen: reichen — to reach (for a thing) (infinitive; nach etwas reichen)
glossary.rein: rein — clear, pure (adj.; hell und rein, of the eyes)
glossary.schloß: das Schloß — castle (1857 spelling of Schloss); also schließen — closed (3rd sg. past: der Ring schloß sich fest an seinen Arm)
glossary.schon: schon — already; also the reassuring particle “right enough, never fear”
glossary.stach: stechen — stabbed, put out (3rd sg. past; ausstechen: stach ihm die Augen aus)
glossary.streifte: streifen — stripped off, slipped off (3rd sg. past; den Ring vom Arm streifen)
glossary.strich: streichen — swept, skimmed along (3rd sg. past; hinstreichen, of a bird in flight — not streichen ‘to spread’)
glossary.todten: der Todte — the dead man (adjective used as a noun, acc. sg.; 1857 spelling of Tote)
glossary.weiß: weiß — white (adj.); also wissen — to know (1st and 3rd sg. pres.: ich weiß, er weiß)
glossary.zog: ziehen — drew, pulled (3rd sg. past; zurückziehen: to draw back); also journeyed (herumziehen: zog weiter in der Welt herum)
